extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework for analyzing state functions that distinguishes between (1) the expression/formulation of the state's will (politics) and (2) the execution of that will (administration), and guidance on what to examine when studying real political systems beyond formal constitutional text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look beyond formal constitutional provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confine study to the Constitution or other formal governmental organization; get back of the formal organization and examine the real political life of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that most writers (often lawyers) err by focusing only on positive law; this method is likely to mislead because a government's character is determined as much by extra-legal as by legal institutions. Anti-pattern: analyzing a system solely by its written constitution and ignoring customs, parties, or informal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include extra-legal institutions in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that extra-legal institutions (customs, parties, cabinets, informal bodies) frequently shape a political system's character and may have more influence than formal legal forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Rome retaining republican forms while functioning as an empire; the English Cabinet being central despite its absence in English law. Guidance: examine parties, customs, and other informal institutions when explaining how government actually operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the administrative system as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative institutions must be examined alongside constitutional provisions because the administrative system has as great an influence on the general governmental system as the constitutional form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gneist's work is cited: parliamentary government cannot be understood apart from English administrative institutions. Anti-pattern: treating administrative matters as secondary or ignoring administrative structures when comparing political systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for de facto constitutional change by political forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Political forces interpret and amend constitutional instruments in practice, so the actual political system can diverge from the written constitution long before formal amendments appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Presidential election practice where parties, not electors' independent judgment, determine outcomes. Guidance: analyze party behavior and practical mechanisms that effectively 'amend' constitutional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: When constitution is unwritten, analyze custom and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In systems without a written constitution, the constitution is largely a matter of custom, so customs and extra-legal institutions must be examined to set forth the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English system is cited as better described by those who study custom as well as law. Guidance: prioritize customary practices and informal rules where positive law is absent or vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the abstraction of the state cautiously but comparatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Because real political systems across peoples at similar stages resemble each other, one can conceive of the state abstractly and compare institutions across systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument: human nature conditions political life and leads to similarity of ends and methods; therefore comparative abstraction is possible. Guidance: use comparative abstraction to identify common functions while checking concrete institutional variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate two primary governmental functions: expression and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Political functions group naturally under two heads: operations necessary to the expression (formulation) of the state's will, and operations necessary to the execution of that will — labelled Politics and Administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politics = formulation/guiding/influencing policy; Administration = execution/application of policy and laws. The distinction is both psychological and economical (division of labor). Use these categories to structure analysis of governmental action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'politics' as formulation/influence of policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics relates to policies or expressions of the state will and involves guiding or influencing governmental policy through party organization, public opinion, patronage, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Century Dictionary quoted: politics includes organizing parties, influencing public opinion, attracting voters, and distributing patronage. Guidance: when assessing political activity, look for these expressive and influence-oriented mechanisms; avoid conflating them with mere administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'administration' as execution of the state's will (broader than 'executive')
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration refers to the duties of executing the state's will: the exercise of powers and duties of government that are neither legislative nor judicial — i.e., public services and application of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution that 'administration' is often used loosely to mean the executive branch; instead treat administration functionally as execution even when exercised by non-executive organs. Guidance: evaluate who actually executes policy (agencies, courts, local bodies), not only who is formally labeled 'executive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of the separation of powers doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's tripartite separation (legislative, executive, judicial) influenced institutions, but in practice the separation of powers and authorities is attenuated and exceptions are frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and constitutions create overlaps; examples: courts make law by deciding cases, executives enact ordinances, legislatures perform administrative functions. Guidance: when applying separation-of-powers analysis, expect 'vicinage' and functional overlap rather than strict compartmentalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze overlapping functions of governmental organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although organs are mainly busied with one function, they often perform parts of the other: executives have ordinance/legislative power; legislatures perform administrative duties; courts make law through adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific U.S. examples: legislature passes special acts performing administration; executive uses veto to influence politics; judges called administrative any power not exclusively one of the three. Guidance: empirical analysis should trace what each organ actually does rather than rely only on formal assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect further differentiation into subordinate and technical authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: As government complexity increases, primary functions subdivide into minor/secondary functions handled by distinct authorities (e.g., judicial authorities, supervisory executive authorities, technical/administrative agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text identifies three kinds of authorities engaged in execution: judicial (apply law in concrete cases), executive (general supervision), and administrative (technical, scientific, commercial activities). Guidance: map these subfunctions and their institutional homes when studying modern governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loose legalistic labeling of 'administrative' powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts habitually label any power not exclusively legislative, executive, or judicial as 'administrative,' which can obscure the functional reality that administration is execution of the state's will and not identical with any single formal organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of judicial looseness, analysts should clarify whether 'administrative' describes function or formal branch. Anti-pattern: treating the court's label 'administrative power' as definitive of who performs execution.
